summary: VS Code is a very large Electron application organised by layer rather than by feature. src/vs splits into base, platform, editor, workbench and sessions, each allowed to depend only on the layers below it. extensions holds the built-in extensions, which use the same public API third parties do, and build, cli and test carry the packaging pipeline, the Rust CLI and the automation suites.

districts.name: The Layered City
districts.purpose: The application: base utilities, platform services, the Monaco editor, the workbench shell and the sessions layer, plus the public API declarations.

districts.name: The Extension Quarter
districts.purpose: Built-in extensions such as git, TypeScript, markdown, emmet and the language features, written against the same API third-party extensions use.

districts.name: The Shipyard
districts.purpose: The packaging pipeline: gulp tasks, per-platform installers, the Azure Pipelines definitions and the bundler configurations.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: Out-of-process suites: smoke tests that drive a real build, the automation driver, sanity checks and component fixtures.

districts.name: The Rust Annex
districts.purpose: The separately compiled command-line launcher and tunnel client, the only Rust in the repository.

districts.name: The Sign Works
districts.purpose: Icons, platform assets and the file associations that make an installed build look native on each operating system.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: Workflows and a large amount of issue automation, which a tracker of this size cannot operate without.

districts.name: The Depot
districts.purpose: Developer entry points: run the app from source, run tests, and the helper scripts contributors call daily.

importantModules.role: The bottom layer: collections, events, disposables, async helpers and DOM utilities, with no dependency on anything above it.
The dependency injection system every service in the product is registered and resolved through.
The Monaco editor's public surface, which is published as a standalone package from this same source.
The text model: the buffer, line handling and decorations that everything in the editor reads from.
The workbench entry point that registers the contributions making up the visible application.
Implements the vscode module extensions import; the boundary between the product and extension code.
The Electron main process entry: lifecycle, windows and the desktop application shell.
The server entry used by remote development and the browser build, sharing the workbench with the desktop app.
The stable extension API declaration; the proposed API files beside it are the staging area for new surface.
The newest top-level layer, documented in place with LAYERS.md and LAYOUT.md describing its own rules.
The built-in git integration, and the clearest example of what the extension API can carry.

strengths: The layer rule is the architecture: base, platform, editor, workbench and sessions may only depend downwards, which is what keeps a codebase this size navigable.
Built-in features are extensions using the public API, so the extension surface is exercised by the product itself.
The same source produces a desktop app, a server for remote development, a browser build and the standalone Monaco editor.
Testing runs at several levels: unit tests inside src, API tests as an extension, and smoke tests that drive a real build through the automation driver.
The proposed API mechanism gives new extension surface a staging area instead of shipping it as stable immediately.
concerns: Nineteen thousand files with src/vs/workbench alone holding nearly five thousand; no newcomer can hold the tree in their head, and the layer documentation is the only usable map.
Over 21,000 open issues and pull requests are attached to the repository, so the tracker is a corpus rather than a work queue.
extensions/copilot is more than half of the extensions directory, which unbalances what looks like a directory of peers.
The repository mixes TypeScript, Rust and several bundlers (gulp, vite, rspack appear side by side under build), so the build story is layered rather than single.
Source and tests are split between in-tree unit tests and the separate test directory, so the suite for a given change is not always obvious.
